before: The missions researchers David Barrett and Todd Johnson used three types, and the *New International Dictionary of Pentecostal and Charismatic Movements* (NIDPCM) uses a similar pattern.

**Classical Pentecostals.** These are the churches and denominations that grew out of the revivals of the early 1900s. This is our family. We teach that a believer can be baptized in the Holy Spirit as an experience after conversion, and that speaking in tongues is the first sign of it. "Classical" does not mean "better." It means "earliest."

**Classical Pentecostals.** This term usually refers to churches and movements that grew from the early 1900s revivals. The historical family is diverse: Trinitarian and Oneness Pentecostals both identify with classical Pentecostal history, though they differ on the doctrine of God. This course represents the Trinitarian classical Pentecostal tradition. Many Trinitarian classical Pentecostal bodies teach that Spirit baptism empowers believers for witness and that speaking in tongues is its initial evidence. "Classical" refers to historical origins, not spiritual superiority.

before: A **broad definition** is favored by the historian and missiologist Allan Anderson. He uses a "family resemblance" approach. Members of a family may look alike even though no single feature is shared by everyone. In the same way, Pentecostal churches share a cluster of features: an emphasis on experiencing the Spirit, belief in healing and in the Spirit's power in daily life, and lively, participatory worship. Not every church has every feature. This lets Anderson include many African, Asian and Latin American churches.

before: Researchers working with the Center for the Study of Global Christianity, including Gina Zurlo, estimate that Pentecostals and charismatics together number more than 660 million people in 2025. Estimates vary mainly because of the definition: a narrow one gives a smaller total, a broad one a larger total. Many countries do not count church members by tradition, and some leaders report numbers that are hopeful rather than checked. A statistic is a careful estimate, not an exact count. We do not measure the work of the Spirit by numbers.

One fact is clear. The majority of Pentecostals and charismatics live in Africa, Latin America and Asia. The center of the movement has moved away from where it started. This is one reason this seminary, which serves pastors in Latin America and Africa, studies the movement closely. Your own churches are part of the story.
after: The World Christian Database estimated about 664 million Pentecostal and charismatic Christians worldwide in 2025. This is a broad estimate that includes Pentecostal, charismatic, and independent-charismatic Christians across different church traditions; it is not a count of classical Pentecostal denomination members alone. Estimates vary with definitions and available records, and some figures rely on self-reported church data. Treat the number as an estimate, not an exact count. We do not measure the work of the Spirit by numbers. (See Gina A. Zurlo, Todd M. Johnson, and Peter F. Crossing, “World Christianity 2025: Regional Perspectives,” and the World Christian Database, “Status of Global Christianity, 2025.”) [U1.4]

before: **Periodicals.** The best known is *The Apostolic Faith*, published by the Azusa Street Mission in Los Angeles from 1906 to 1908. It reported meetings, printed testimonies, and told readers what the mission believed. It is a priceless source because it comes from the time of the events. Its limit is that the mission published it to encourage readers and spread the message. It shows what the editors chose to print, not everything that happened.

before: **A single origin: Azusa Street.** The movement began at the Azusa Street Mission in Los Angeles in 1906, under William J. Seymour, an African American preacher. Many people traveled there and carried the message across the world. Seymour had been taught by Charles Parham, who in 1901 in Topeka, Kansas, had taught that tongues were the sign of Spirit baptism. This story honors a real center of influence. Its limit is that it can hide what was happening elsewhere.

**Many origins at the same time.** The Spirit was moving in many places in the same years. At the Mukti mission in India, led by Pandita Ramabai, a revival with prayer and spiritual gifts took place in 1905, and the missionary Minnie Abrams wrote about it. In Chile in 1909, a revival began among Methodists in Valparaiso under Willis Hoover. Pentecostalism is then not one stream from one spring but many streams that joined. Its limit is that it can make the real influence of Azusa Street seem smaller than it was.

**Holiness and Wesleyan roots.** John Wesley taught that believers could seek a deeper holiness, sometimes called entire sanctification. In the 1800s the Holiness movement carried this hope forward, and others added the Keswick teaching on a life filled with the Spirit and belief in divine healing. Many early Pentecostal leaders came from Holiness churches. Historians such as Vinson Synan and Donald Dayton stress these roots. Its limit is that it may not explain what was truly new in the early 1900s.

before: Pentecostalism is a large, varied and mostly majority-world movement of three types: classical Pentecostal, charismatic, and neo-charismatic or independent. A narrow definition centers on Spirit baptism with tongues; Allan Anderson's broad "family resemblance" approach includes many more churches. Estimates place the total at more than 660 million in 2025, though numbers vary with definition. Historians use periodicals, testimonies, denominational records, oral history and statistics, and each has limits. The origin story may be told as a single origin at Azusa Street, as many origins such as Mukti in 1905 and Chile in 1909, or as the fruit of Holiness and Wesleyan roots. Pentecostals hold that the true origin is Pentecost in Acts 2, and that Azusa Street and the related revivals were a genuine work of God. We answer cessationist and other evangelical objections from Scripture, and we hold our convictions with humility.

## Review and Reflection
1. Compare the narrow and broad definitions of Pentecostalism. What does each help historians see, and what does each leave out?
2. Which kinds of sources are used in this unit, and what is one limitation of each?
3. Explain why the 2025 global estimate should not be read as a count of classical Pentecostal denomination members.
